For a long time, I've wished that I could offer a form of SSO to my friends and family, so that different people could transparently be granted authorization to view different sides of my family and me, all without needing to tell them in advance about it. So, for instance, maybe I would have some kind of sign-in/sign-up form, and the sign-up would ask questions one after another, in a way that triangulated who they were and how we knew each other without giving things away, until they established their proximity to me some how. Basically, I'm thinking that I could grant people an SSO account ahead of when they created it, and they could choose to take it or not. It would be like telling the concierge of one's building, "if you ever see this person, let them in ..."

I've been picturing that each piece would have a different sort of representation than the one most people are familiar with. Usually, one finds that audio files have a player with a play button on the left, a play bar in the center, and the play bar goes from left to right. Instead, I'd have something more like a type of loom that goes from top to bottom.
a new sort of representation of multidimensional streamed media, the top-down, multi-fingered river loom

There would be several channels of audio vertically oriented, scrolling by like a river, as though the webpage were a portal onto a river that was flowing from top to bottom, only it would actually be multiple rivers - some of them audio, some of them control structures, for example, each manipulated or automated CC value would be its own river. it would change thickness, thinness based on its expression. For some di-pole controls like audio pan, it would flip right vs left with a line down the center. For example, on the microfreak control structures that can modulate one thing with another on a grid, it would be

There's something special about radio. I remember making short-wave radio as a kid from an electronics kit. I climbed out the window and drove a screwdriver in the earth to ground the kit. I had a single earpiece that pulled in signals from far across the country. I felt like I was talking to distant planets. I wanted to say back, "I'm here, too." I always wanted to get into ham radio, and even started studying the test for it as a kid, thinking that might be in the cards, but it failed to materialize.

Whoz, pronounced "whooze," sells a workforce optimization platform to IT services, consulting, and engineering firms. It maps what each person in a services firm can do, matches them to open projects, and schedules the work. The company headlines it as "AI-Driven Workforce Optimization. Built to Scale."
One AI agent staffs the whole organization
Whoz gives a customer firm a single managing agent that assigns every worker in it.
One AI agent staffs the whole organization

The Whoz home page, read on 2026-09-22 Tue, sells the platform on "agent-led orchestration": "Leverage AI and agent-led orchestration to map skills, match talent to projects, and optimize scheduling for complex, large-scale operations." It addresses the firm as the owner of one agent — "Your AI agent delivers instant, accurate talent matching for every opportunity."
One AI agent staffs the whole organization
Talent Cloud — a map of the workforce's skills, meant to surface people a staffing manager would otherwise miss.
Business & Staffing Studio — where a staffer assigns people to projects and balances their load.
Performance Analytics — reporting on billable rates and utilization.
Whoz AImplify — the AI layer: skill matching, generated profiles, suggested candidates.
Integrations & Workflows — connections to the systems a firm already runs.
Privacy by Design — how Whoz handles the employee data the platform holds.

Twenty-one people founded Whoz in 2016. Its Why Whoz page tells the story as consultants who got tired of staffing spreadsheets: "What if we developed it ourselves? Pretty soon, there was no looking back. Whoz becomes the largest start-up in history, with twenty-one founders!"
The same page says the team "work[s] from cities all across France," and claims "500 k+ users worldwide" and "30 millions euros raised in Series A."

A wireframe is a simplified visual plan for an interface. It shows page or screen structure, content hierarchy, and the placement of important controls so people can reason about how the experience is organized.
Wireframes make competing layouts quick to compare and help a team discuss information order, navigation, and user tasks before visual styling takes center stage.
They can be sketches on paper or digital diagrams. Their level of detail depends on the question being explored; a wireframe may also show a sequence of screens or key interaction states.
A wireframe emphasizes structure and hierarchy. A Mock/Up emphasizes visual treatment such as typography, color, imagery, and spacing.
A prototype lets people try some of the proposed behavior. A wireframe can remain static or be connected into a simple flow for early testing.
These artifacts are often revisited as people learn more about the user, the product, and its technical constraints.

WireGuard is a VPN protocol and implementation that presents an encrypted tunnel as an ordinary network interface. It carries IP packets inside UDP and aims to be simpler and faster than older VPNs such as OpenVPN and IPsec, with a small enough codebase to audit.
It began on Linux and now runs on Windows, macOS, BSD, iOS and Android. The kernel components are licensed GPLv2.
Tailscale builds its Tailscale/Tailnet on WireGuard, using the userspace Go implementation wireguard-go, and adds key distribution, sign-in, NAT traversal and access control around it.
Small and opinionated. One fixed set of modern primitives instead of negotiated cipher suites: Curve25519, ChaCha20, Poly1305, BLAKE2, SipHash24 and HKDF, arranged with the Noise protocol framework.
Peers identified by public keys. Each peer holds a private key and lists the public keys of the peers it will accept. Packets are encrypted to a peer's public key and sent to its endpoint.
Roaming. A peer's endpoint can change, for example when a laptop switches between networks, without rebuilding the tunnel.

WireGuard itself does not distribute keys or discover peers. Plain WireGuard requires each peer's keys and endpoints to be configured by hand. A coordination layer, such as Tailscale's, automates that step.
WireGuard is not Tailscale. WireGuard is the tunnel protocol, and Tailscale is a service that manages many WireGuard tunnels as one network.
